EntertainmentTab.title: Natalie Imbruglia on her worst audition: 'I remember feeling icky'
EntertainmentTab.text:
When it comes to writing music, Natalie Imbruglia needs constant motion.

"I walk around in circles to get the melodies, to catch them," the Australian singer says.

"If I'm sat in a chair, I get nothing.

"So if I go and work with someone new and they have a shoebox-sized studio, I'm like, 'How am I going to do my circles?'"

Imbruglia doesn't know exactly how many laps she completed during the making of her dancefloor-ready seventh album, Algorithm. But it was a lot.

Inspired by Talking Heads and Grace Jones, it's a record whose shimmering surfaces disguise lyrics of deep emotional complexity.

On Who Dimmed The Lights, the 51-year-old addresses how her mental health "unravelled" as she went through perimenopause.

"It was really tough," she says. "Perimenopause is not just about hormones. It's to do with your mind. Your brain needs oestrogen to function, so when the levels fluctuate, it affects your spatial awareness.

"I've never walked into so many doorways. The brain fog's quite jarring."

Doorways weren't the only problem. Imbruglia says perimenopause exacerbated her ADHD, which she was diagnosed with in midlife. Other symptoms included heightened anxiety and anger.

"You start seeing an expression on other people of, like, 'What's happening to you?'

"I was seeing that face a lot, and it's to do with your ability to process [information]. Your fuse is shorter."

Things came to a head on tour, where her stage fright went into overdrive and she suffered "just terrible, terrible anxiety".

"I become sensitive to sound, so it feels like you're screaming at me if you're talking normally," she says. "I can't process questions very well. I act twitchy and weird, and it seemed to get worse with perimenopause."

She says her behaviour became a "nightmare" for her team. Pressed for an example, she explains: "If you asked me whether I wanted still or sparkling water, I'd say, 'That's a question, and I can't answer questions right now'.

"How diva is that?"

Well, it's not exactly Mariah Carey demanding baskets of puppies and forbidding eye contact, but Imbruglia was shaken up.

The day after one concert, she told her co-writers David Sneddon and Anu Pillai, "Guys, I think I'm going to have to quit my job because I can't cope with how I'm treating people before the show."

They helped to talk her down, putting her fight-or-flight instincts into context.

"What they helped me realise is that I was trying to stop the behaviour with willpower, and if I just relaxed into it and said to myself, 'You know, you're about to perform in front of a lot of people, it's natural that you're nervous', maybe I wouldn't be resisting it as much."

The impromptu therapy session inspired a new song, Upside Down, external - but Imbruglia is understandably frustrated that perimenopause isn't more widely understood, saying many women are rejected by their GP when they seek HRT treatment.

"My mum never talked to me about it," she reflects, "but looking back, I know she had a really bad one.

"Her anxiety was off the charts, too, and I have a lot more compassion now, because she had four kids. I've only got one."

As a child in Sydney, Imbruglia was drawn to performing. She'd squeeze lemon on her hair to make it blonder, and put on concerts of Whitney Houston covers for her neighbours.

Before long, she was cast in commercials for Coca-Cola and Twisties, and spent her Christmases singing carols in shopping centres.

"But when you turn 15 or 16, and you're into boys, you're like, 'Oh, that's really naff. I don't want to be doing that any more'," she laughs.

From that point onwards, Imbruglia became "basically unparentable".

"I was sneaking out and sleeping in someone's car on the beach, then getting busted.

"My parents were really strict - and my mum would turn up at parties with my picture, going, 'Have you seen this girl?'

"Socially, it was a disaster."

Music continued to be her solace. Dating a drummer, she switched allegiance from Whitney Houston to Tom Waits and Tori Amos, but the urge to sing remained.

You can see that hunger in a recently rediscovered photograph of a pre-fame Imbruglia, external, pressed up against the barriers of an INXS concert in 1992.

"It was my first ever concert," she says. "I was 15. I had white, tight jeans on."

In the photo, "everyone else is screaming but I'm looking at (Michael Hutchence) with this determination in my eyes.

"I'm studying him, like, 'How can I be up there too?'"

She got her chance in 1997 after quitting her role as builder's apprentice Beth Brennan in Aussie soap Neighbours.

Moving to London, she signed a deal with RCA Records and immediately scored an international hit with her first single, Torn.

Famously, the song was a cover – a fact journalists never let her forget, even though she co-wrote every other track on her debut album, Left of the Middle (lifetime sales, seven million copies).

"Yeah, I got famous on a song that I didn't write," she says now, "but there's more to what you bring to a song than whether you wrote the lyrics."

She still loves the song – "Torn was a beautiful gift" – but the furore around it fuelled her insecurities.

As a result, she essentially self-sabotaged her career. The lead single from her second album, That Day, was a free-verse stream-of-consciousness that sounded like a manic inner monologue.

"That was my rebellion against Torn," she says. "It doesn't have a chorus.

"That was my way of going, 'Can I get on with my life now? I've just started learning the craft of songwriting, I'm young, I didn't ask for this'."

In the midst of the madness, she auditioned for the lead role of Satine in Baz Luhrmann's Moulin Rouge – which counts as one of the stranger experiences of her career.

"The audition was, pretty much, 'Have an orgasm'," she grimaces. "Because I think that happens in the movie." (Indeed, Satine delivers a breathy boudoir monologue, external as she tries to seduce Ewan McGregor's character, Christian.)

But Imbruglia stresses it wasn't a creepy casting couch situation.

"It's Baz, that doesn't really fit," she says of the soft-hearted director.

"But I remember leaving and feeling really icky. Like, 'Ohhh, that was awful. Where's my mummy?'"

Back in the world of music, Imbruglia returned to more commercial sounds on hits like Wrong Impression (2002) and Shiver (2005). But sales dwindled and her fourth album was shelved by her label.

In the years that followed, she joined the Australian version of The X Factor and appeared in a UK production of Alan Ayckbourn's play Things We Do for Love, before making a tentative return to music with covers album Male (2015); and the more personal, introspective Firebird (2021).

"It was quitting music and coming back to it that gave me an appreciation of my abilities," she says.

"I might not be the best songwriter, even now, but there's only one me, and when I go inside myself and feel the emotion of what I'm writing about and deliver it, that's what my fans resonate with, and that's enough."

She certainly has a lot to say on Algorithm. As well as the frank discussion of mental health, the title track talks about her flirtation with internet conspiracy theories.

She won't say which ones ("I think it's irresponsible") but stresses the danger is omnipresent.

"There's a voice in my head that says, 'You don't want to click on that', and I'll click on it. It's like this compulsion.

"You have to change the settings. Don't allow yourself to be in a situation where your stress relief is scrolling on a phone in bed. It's just not healthy."

Ultimately, however, the album ends on a note of positivity.

Beautiful Love, external, co-written with Snow Patrol's Gary Lightbody, is a soaring hymn to embracing your flaws and making peace with life's highs and lows.

"I've always made the joke that I'll never be a Buddhist because it's a middle path," she smiles.

"I like the pendulum to swing. Whether it's extreme joy or extreme pain, I like to feel the experience of life."

EntertainmentTab.title: TV presenter Sarah Khalifa sentenced to death in Egypt drugs case
EntertainmentTab.text:
Egyptian television presenter Sarah Khalifa and 11 other people have been sentenced to death by hanging after being convicted of drugs charges.

According to state-owned al-Ahram newspaper, they were part of a criminal gang which imported ingredients used to make drugs with the intent of selling them.

They also had illegal firearms and munitions.

Khalifa, 39, is best known for her TV programme Mission Impossible which dealt with crime issues. She has denied the charges.

Nine fellow defendants have been sentenced to life imprisonment, while seven have been acquitted.

Khalifa's lawyer said she would appeal the death sentence.

The verdict was first announced last month.

However, it was only confirmed a month later after the court obtained a religious opinion from the grand mufti of Egypt - a legal requirement in death sentence cases.

During the trial, the court heard that authorities had seized more than 750kg (1,653lbs) of narcotics and the imported raw materials to make them.

Twenty witnesses had given statements to the prosecutors, al-Ahram said, in addition to electronic evidence that included conversations and video clips.

According to the state-run Akhbar al-Youm newspaper, when asked by the judge about her alleged role during a court appearance last September, Khalifa said she had never seen any drugs until she was photographed with them inside the anti-narcotics authority offices.

According to a 2025 Amnesty International report, there were 492 death sentences in the course of the year, 23 of which were carried out., external.

The defendants were found guilty of drug trafficking and rape, "crimes that did not amount to 'intentional killing' to which the use of the death penalty must be restricted under international law and standards", the report said.

EntertainmentTab.title: Union J star from Newmarket swaps stage for racecourse
EntertainmentTab.text:
A former X Factor contestant and boy band member says his return to horse racing feels like a full-circle moment as he swaps the stage for the racecourse.

Before finding fame with pop group Union J, JJ Hamblett, who grew up in Newmarket in Suffolk, spent his youth horse racing and gained his jockey licence at 16.

His first competitive appearance came at Doncaster Racecourse in 2005 and on 11 September, he will return there to take part in The Leger Legends race.

"It's like I've done this huge 360 and gone back to where I started, which is going to be very unusual next week," said the 38-year-old.

"I've loved being back in horse racing and I've kind of got that buzz back again."

Growing up around horses and with his father a jockey, the singer said he loved ponies and eventually started riding racehorses at 14 years old.

"Whenever we wasn't at school, we would kind of want to always be riding horses," Hamblett said about himself and his brother.

"And when I wasn't riding, I was in my room and singing karaoke... singing a bit of Westlife and Boyzone."

He recalled filming himself singing using a VHS recorder as a child. When he later watched the tape with his family, they discovered he had accidentally recorded over all of their childhood videos.

"I always kind of loved singing, and that was also my passion," Hamblett said.

The singer said he wanted something "extra" in his career and that he was "missing that buzz" with horse racing.

"I'm quite tall for a jockey, I'm 5ft 9in (1.75m)... but I did struggle with my weight, so I got to the point where I was about 8st 9lb (55kg) which does seem light in hindsight, but it was quite heavy," he added.

"I was trying to keep my weight down all the time and struggling driving up to Scotland for one ride, and the opportunities weren't there at the time."

He went on to try acting before deciding to join an online platform for people in the creative industry. His future bandmate Jaymi Hensley then got in touch.

"To this day, he says, 'The only reason I let you in is because you had a six pack,'" Hamblett added.

The band initially formed as a trio called Triple J in 2011 before they auditioned in the ninth series of The X Factor.

George Shelley joined as the group's fourth member during the competition and the band, renamed Union J, went on to finish fourth under judge Louis Walsh.

"I'm very, very excited for the race, but I know on the day it's going to be extremely nerve-racking," Hamblett said.

He said he would not go back to racing full time but if he were to win the Leger Legends event he would want to defend the title, and if he did not win, he would want to enter again to try and win.

The singer also hinted at a potential Union J reunion to celebrate the band's 15th anniversary.

"Definitely next year Union J will be back doing more shows and festivals," he said.

EntertainmentTab.title: The Grand Tour's new presenters: 'I hope we prove the critics wrong'
EntertainmentTab.text:
For more than two decades, Top Gear and The Grand Tour were defined as much by the three men presenting them as by the cars they drove.

Jeremy Clarkson, Richard Hammond and James May built one of television's most recognisable partnerships, meaning anyone taking over The Grand Tour was always going to face a daunting task.

Now YouTubers James Engelsman and Thomas Holland and, perhaps most unexpectedly, train enthusiast-turned-internet star Francis Bourgeois are stepping into their shoes for the new series.

And, with initial reviews generally mixed, they knew they had some convincing to do.

"They literally changed the car world," Holland says of the previous trio.

He understands why some fans have questions about whether the show should continue with anyone else.

"They're completely justified to feel that, because they did the same thing that we did - which is grow up watching Clarkson, Hammond and May.

"The show was a very important part of our lives as car enthusiasts."

Engelsman says they themselves initially had many of the same doubts that viewers will have.

"We've had all the same reactions that the audience has had to every part of this process like, 'Who would do that? What an idiot.'

"We've been through it all and we're just lucky enough to have come out the other side and realised, 'OK, this is actually all stuff that could work.'"

"Now we've filmed it, I'm just excited to show the world," Bourgeois says. "We've done our absolute best and the critics will be critics and I hope that we will prove them wrong."

Holland adds that he hopes people will give the show a chance before judging.

"Have a watch and if you don't like it, you're well within your rights, I can't force anyone to like anything."

For a show built around the chemistry of its three former presenters, finding a replacement trio with such chemistry was always going to be as important as finding people who knew about cars.

Engelsman and Holland are an already established double act as the presenters of Throttle House, a motoring YouTube channel with more than three million subscribers.

The bigger unknown was who would become their third presenter.

That search eventually led the show's producers to Francis Bourgeois, a social media star better known for standing on railway platforms than behind the wheel of a supercar.

Engelsman says he and Holland had done chemistry testing with a number of people, but Bourgeois immediately felt different.

"As soon as Francis showed up, we were like: 'That guy'," Holland says.

Bourgeois remembers their first meeting taking place on a leather sofa in a hotel outside Basingstoke, where they mostly talked about what cars they owned.

By the time filming began, Holland says there was no need to consciously work out how to make the three-person dynamic function as "it just worked and clicked immediately".

While the chemistry came quickly, actually finding out they had the job was much less straightforward. Engelsman says there was "no immediate moment" when they were formally told they had been chosen.

"It was the most gradual thing," he says.

He and Holland initially thought they were simply part of a wider audition process, but then found themselves repeatedly being invited into writers' rooms and asked for their views on ideas for the show.

For Bourgeois, that uncertainty may have been helpful as he admits he'd "just fall apart and start crying" if he'd found out about the job.

There is a clear generational shift with the new presenters, all three of whom built their profiles on social media - and critics have been mixed on how successfully that translates to The Grand Tour.

The Independent's three-star review, external described the reboot as "all rather safe" and said the presenters feel "stilted".

The Guardian's review, external agreed and called the trio a "decent, if slightly anonymous, presence" who seem "quite meek and pleasant, and without any obvious dynamic".

But it did praise Bourgeois, with Stuart Heritage calling him "the most enthusiastic enthusiast currently working on planet Earth".

The FT also awarded the show three-stars, external and said that while the big budget spectacles are enjoyable to watch, they also feel "a little muted".

It added that "the real question is whether a series that has been driven by big personalities like Clarkson, May and Hammond can survive with a new team".

Hammond tells BBC News he tuned in for The Grand Tour's return and said it was great to see the new team getting going.

"That's the most important thing for them is to make their show. We made our show and we're really good at being us. They're going to be really good at being them," he says.

Hammond says the audience need to "give them the chance" to show that.

Bourgeois may be best known for his ecstatic trainspotting videos but he says his love of cars goes back just as far.

Growing up near Willesden Junction in London, there were plenty of trains to watch, but he was also fascinated by the cars outside his home.

"There was a particular Mitsubishi Legnum VR-4 that was outside my parents' flat window and I just loved it," he tells me. "I suppose with my social media, I'm just showing one of my passions and I have really wanted to let out that car enthusiasm too.

"It's nice that these two sides of my very strong passions are in harmony together and it's been a real pleasure to drive some of the cars on The Grand Tour."

His enthusiasm for transport more generally has already rubbed off on his co-presenters who say they've become "very educated by Francis on many things during long walks and long drives".

Bourgeois is even lobbying for The Grand Tour to devote an episode to another of his interests: power stations. And he has found a surprisingly receptive audience in Clarkson.

When the new trio met their predecessors, Bourgeois says seeing Clarkson in person gave him "a flutter in my tummy" and the pair bonded, inevitably, over trains, before moving on to power stations, and a lengthy discussion about cheeseburgers.

Engelsman says all three former presenters were supportive of their successors and "were very paternal and caring about it".

"They all seemed quite excited for there to be a new iteration," Engelsman says, adding that Clarkson even told them: "We'll look after you".

EntertainmentTab.title: Jay-Z: Stars join US rapper at long-awaited UK show
EntertainmentTab.text:
Jay-Z's first headline solo show in the UK in more than a decade saw him celebrate hip-hop culture alongside a host of special guests, including Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and Giggs.

The US rap superstar rolled back the years for more than two hours - playing hits like 99 Problems, Empire State of Mind and Dead Presidents - as he took to the stage at Tottenham Hotspur Stadium on Friday night for the first of two shows in London this weekend.

The run is part of his Jay-Z 30 tour, which is marking the 30th anniversary of his debut album, Reasonable Doubt, and his culture-shaping career that followed.

Fans of his wife Beyoncé had hoped she would join him on stage, like she did at two of his three New York shows this summer, as she was also celebrating her 45th birthday on Friday.

The show's opening set the tone for the star-studded evening to follow, as British actor Sir Idris Elba kicked things off by performing the intro track to his 2007 album, American Gangster.

As Jay-Z took to the stage, he recalled coming to London in 1989 with his mentor Jaz-O and seeing "what was possible" and it became a "special" place in his career.

His return to the capital this time round was explosive, with the rapper rattling through a string of hits like Izzo (H.O.V.A.), On To The Next One and Song Cry.

Throughout the show, vintage video clips and moments from his early career played across a massive LED screen, while an orchestra and a few guitarists accompanied him on stage.

There was no sign of Rihanna or Alicia Keys, who both made appearances during the New York run for their collaboration tracks, but the crowd made up for their absence by chanting back their lyrics during Run This Town and Empire State of Mind.

Jay-Z also took a moment to thank his fans who have been there from the beginning, telling them that "music saved my life".

His reflective mood continued as he performed Hard Knock Life (Ghetto Anthem) and Where I'm From, which explores his upbringing in the Marcy housing projects in Brooklyn, New York.

He cranked the energy back up for his 2011 hit No Church in the Wild, which was amplified by fiery pyrotechnics that radiated heat through the stadium.

Originally a collaboration with controversial rapper Ye, also known as Kanye West, Jay-Z left his voice in for the chorus but cut his verses out.

US DJ Khaled had a brief moment on stage while Jay-Z changed, but it was the appearance of London-born rapper Giggs which got the crowd erupting.

He appeared overwhelmed at one stage, his hand clutching his face, as he took in the packed crowd while performing his track Talkin Da Hardest alongside Jay-Z.

The surprise guests didn't stop there, as Lauryn Hill and Wyclef Jean from the 90s American hip-hop collective The Fugees reunited to perform their hit tracks Ready or Not, Killing Me Softly with His Song and Fu-Gee-La.

It was a full-circle moment for both them and Jay-Z as he recalled supporting them on their European tour.

The US rap superstar closed out the night with rousing renditions of Public Service Announcement (Interlude) and Numb/Encore, hailing it as a "legendary night" that he would "never forget".

The crowd appeared to agree as thousands praised him by holding up his famous diamond hand gesture.

Fans had travelled from across the UK and the world to see the rapper, including Prince Dean Sithole, who hailed Jay-Z as one of his role models.

"I think he's very impacting, especially for us black people because we don't get a lot of recognition," the 19-year-old from Leeds told BBC Newsbeat.

"Seeing him today shows that dreams are possible and you can be that person that you want to be."

Jay-Z, real name Shawn Carter, broke through with his 1996 debut album, but it was his third record, Vol. 2: Hard Knock Life, in 1998 which landed him the top spot in the US charts for the first time and a best rap album Grammy.

He went on to establish himself as one of the most influential figures in hip-hop, releasing 13 solo studio albums and several collaboration records, which have secured him 25 Grammy Awards.

He was also the first rapper inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 2017, as well as being inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2021.

Over the years, he has also become one of the most prominent music moguls in the world, with his company Roc Nation representing a host of top talent and, in recent years, it has been behind the Super Bowl half-time show.

In 2019, he was declared hip-hop's first billionaire by Forbes, having built an empire based on music, property, fashion and investments alongside his wife Beyoncé.

The power couple have three children, daughter Blue Ivy, 14, and nine-year-old twins, Rumi and Sir.

EntertainmentTab.title: Richard O'Sullivan: Man About the House star dies aged 82
EntertainmentTab.text:
Actor Richard O'Sullivan, whose roles included Robin Tripp in 1970s TV sitcoms Man About the House and Robin's Nest, has died aged 82.

He was also known for starring in Doctor at Large, Dick Turpin, and the 1980s sitcom Me and My Girl, alongside Tim Brooke-Taylor, Joanne Ridley and Joan Sanderson.

O'Sullivan died surrounded by close family at Brinsworth House, the Royal Variety Charity's care home, in west London where he had lived for 23 years.

In a statement, Giles Cooper of the Royal Variety Charity said: "Richard O'Sullivan was a master of effortless charm and impeccable comic timing, bringing pure warmth, wit, and unforgettable joy to millions of living rooms as a true giant of British television."

Cooper added O'Sullivan would be "sorely missed by us all at the Royal Variety Charity".

The actor's son James O'Sullivan said in his own statement: "My dad was as funny and charming in real life as he appeared on our TV screens over the years.

"Although much of his career happened before I was born, I was fortunate enough to be able to enjoy and witness his incredible talents on the countless re-runs of his shows that made him the respected and loved actor that he was."

He thanked the staff at Brinsworth House for their "love, kindness and care".

Man About the House co-starred Paula Wilcox, Sally Thomsett, Yootha Joyce and Brian Murphy in six series on ITV.

It was about a man sharing a London flat with two single women - quite a daring storyline for that era.

In Me and My Girl, he played a widow living with his adolescent daughter.

Born in London in 1944, O'Sullivan started his career as a child actor in the 50s and 60s, playing uncredited roles in dramas in 1953.

He went on to appear, external in the Children's Film Foundation's first serial production Raiders of the River, and in 1956 he was in Sir Peter Hall's production of Love's Labour's Lost at the Royal Shakespeare Theatre Stratford.

He also appeared in 1961 film Spare the Rod, a social commentary drama about a teacher working in a tough, deprived area, starring Max Bygraves and Donald Pleasance. O'Sullivan played a difficult and defiant student in his final year.

After gaining steady work in dramatic roles, including 1963's Cleopatra, as Pharoah Ptolemy XIII, which starred Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton, he moved towards comedy, in shows such as The Ronnie Barker Playhouse, in 1968, and The Galton and Simpson Comedy the following year.

O'Sullivan was also in two films with Sir Cliff Richard in the 1960s – The Young Ones in 1961 and Wonderful Life in 1964.

By 1973, he took his starring role in Man About the House, which was a big success, not least because of its daring plot about a man living with two single women.

"The issue was not the living arrangement itself, but what it implied," British Comedy Classics said, external of the series.

"A man sharing a flat with two unmarried women would be read as sexual, and that risked the show being rejected or framed as inappropriate for prime-time viewing."

In order to bypass any potential disapproval from their landlords, George and Mildred Roper, who also got their own spin-off TV series, the two women claim their flatmate Robin is gay.

Robin keeps up the pretence for their landlords, which created the comedy and made it acceptable watching for a pre-watershed 70s audience.

Between 1979 and 1982 he took on the more dramatic titlular role of 18th Century highwayman Dick Turpin, in ITV's series.

But by the 80s he returned to sitcoms with Me and My Girl, which ran from 1984 to 1988, and Trouble in Mind in 1991, about a married psychiatrist who is having something of a mid-life crisis.

After this his career became much quieter, with an appearance in Noel's House Party and a starring role in a 1996 film called Holed, about a golfing match.

In his statement, James O'Sullivan concluded: "Always kind-spirited, good humoured, a doting grandfather and a wonderful dad – I will miss him dearly."

EntertainmentTab.title: Russell Howard 'devastated' after his baby son died hours after birth
EntertainmentTab.text:
This story contains content which some readers might find distressing

Comedian Russell Howard has revealed his baby son Felix died earlier this year, shortly after his wife Cerys had given birth.

In a statement, he said he and his wife had faced "unimaginable heartache" and described it as "the most devastating time of our lives".

Howard praised the "extraordinary compassion, kindness and humanity" of the hospital staff who cared for them over the period that followed Felix's death.

He also announced the launch of a new foundation in their late son's name to help families going through similar ordeals, with a comedy fundraiser set to take place next year.

In a statement posted on his social media accounts, external on Friday, Howard recalled: "During our time in hospital, Felix was placed in a cool cot, which meant that my wife and I were able to spend precious hours with our beautiful boy.

"We could hold him, talk to him and tell him how much we loved him. Those hours are among the most precious memories we have of Felix."

Howard and his wife had not publicly announced at the time that they were expecting their second child.

He explained he and his wife had been assigned a bereavement midwife named Lauren, who had experienced a similar tragedy and retrained in order to help other families.

"Her care meant more to us than we could ever put into words," Howard said.

"We were overwhelmed by the care we received, and we made a promise to each other: that we would try to help other families who find themselves facing the same devastating circumstances."

As a result, Howard said he and Cerys were launching The Felix Foundation, which will aim to help families affected by miscarriage, premature birth, stillbirth, neonatal death or related bereavement.

A fundraising event, titled the Stand-Up Gala, will take place at London's O2 Arena in February to raise money for the charity,

Michael McIntyre, Jimmy Carr, Aisling Bea, John Bishop and Mo Gilligan are among the comics who will perform at the event.

Howard said he would "never forget the generosity" of his fellow comics, who were giving their time to the show "completely free of charge".

The 46-year-old is one of the best known stand-up comics in the UK, having appeared on shows such as Mock The Week and Russell Howard's Good News.

The comedian and his wife Cerys, an NHS doctor, have been together since 2004 and share another son, who was born in August 2024.

Howard recently played a string of shows at the Edinburgh Fringe festival, and is currently on a stand-up tour of the UK.

EntertainmentTab.title: How Oasis fans cracked the Celtic Park gigs code in chip shop video
EntertainmentTab.text:
Oasis fans have uncovered a set of cryptic clues in a promo video from the band, suggesting that they will stage gigs at Celtic Park in Glasgow next year.

The Manchester rockers released the 23-second teaser on their social media accounts, showing two boys in what appears to be a Scottish chip shop.

Internet sleuths spotted sets of numbers in posters around the chippy which they worked out to be the map co-ordinates for Celtic's Parkhead stadium.

It has fuelled speculation that the band will be playing at the venue next year- possibly as the first date of a new tour.

It follows the Gallagher brothers' hugely successful reunion tour which saw them perform at 41 sold-out stadium shows in 14 countries.

This included three dates at Murrayfield Stadium, Edinburgh, in August 2025, when they played to 200,000 fans.

The clues hinting at a Celtic Park gig include an advert for a £55.84 family chippy bundle and a poster for radio station Sol FM 98 92.

The numbers spell out the 55.849892N latitude of the stadium.

There is also a sticker on the fridge saying it should be kept at -4, a poster saying the daily special is priced at £2.05 and a taxi number featuring the area code 638.

These numbers together are -4.205638W - Celtic Park's longitude.

Other Scottish clues include the actor Robert Carlyle, who features in the video for Oasis song Little by Little which plays on a TV in the background.

The chip shop fridge is filled with Irn Bru and other AG Barr brands.

One of the boys also hands over a Mars Bar to be deep fried - a Scottish chippy delicacy.

Fans have also posted theories about other "clues" on social media.

One said the position of the two boys is similar to the positions of Noel and Liam Gallagher on the front of the Definitely Maybe album, with the fridge being in a similar position to the window.

Celtic Park has not hosted any concerts for a number of years with the last being Wet, Wet Wet in 1997.

Other noteable gigs there have been Rod Stewart, Status Quo and Joe Cocker in 1991, Bryan Adams and Prince in 1992, U2 and Utah Saints in 1993.

Rod Stewart performed there again in 2014 during the Opening Ceremony for the Commonwealth Games.

Glasgow's Hampden Park has become the city's main concert stadium over the past three decades.

EntertainmentTab.title: 'Not only did I survive, I thrived' - Meera Syal after assaults
EntertainmentTab.text:
Dame Meera Syal has said she "almost gave up" her career after being sexually harassed and assaulted by two "predators" within the media industry.

"I was out of work, I was homeless, sleeping on people's floors, and then these two things happened in quite quick succession," the Wolverhampton-born star said in a candid interview with BBC Asian Network's Amber Haque.

In her new memoir, Vigilauntie, which was published on Thursday, the actress shared that both incidents happened in her 20s, as she was struggling to secure a role.

Now aged 65, she has opened up about the harrowing experiences and reflected on how she overcame them to become one of the most well-known faces on British TV.

"It could have been a point where I gave up," she explained.

"It put some fire in my belly because the reason I wanted to tell these stories is that I did survive, and not only did I survive, I thrived.

"The anger of the injustice of the situation made me seek out a bunch of women that changed the course of my life."

Syal described the first incident as "my first casting couch approach".

She wrote that the man, a theatre director, insinuated he would give her a role in a pantomime if she engaged in sexual acts with him. She refused and was able to leave.

However, a few weeks later an older male actor invited her to his home under the guise that he would help her progress with her career. Instead he assaulted her, she wrote in her book.

The predatory actor has since died.

The comedy star, known for shows including Goodness Gracious Me and The Kumars at No 42, did not report the incidents to the police and did not tell family or friends as it "was the culture" of the industry at the time.

She recalled: "When I have talked about this incident to other women, particularly of my age, they've all said that happened to me and a lot of them have never talked about it because it was part of the culture.

"The 70s, 80s and 90s, it was absolutely part of the culture.

"You wouldn't even bother to report half of these things because A, you wouldn't be believed and B, everyone was doing it."

Joining the BBC in the 1990s, she rose to prominence as part of the team behind the broadcaster's sketch comedy, Goodness Gracious Me!

In 1993, she wrote the screenplay for the comedy-drama film Bhaji On The Beach, and two years later she starred in the Channel 4 romantic comedy film, Beautiful Thing.

The award-winner was a key writer and actress on the 1996 show, and later helped to bring Bollywood to the West End, by co-writing Andrew Lloyd Webber's Bombay Dreams in 2002.

You can listen to the full interview with Dame Meera Syal on Asian Network Trending on BBC Sounds.

If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line.

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘On the other side of pain there can be renewal’: Ezra Collective’s Femi Koleoso on reasons to hold on to hope
EntertainmentTab.text:
My first thought when contacted about guest editing the culture section in today’s Saturday magazine was: this will elevate me into an intellectual bracket far beyond my wildest dreams. The first person I told was my dad. The second was my secondary school English teacher, Mr Pickering. I guess it was a subtle way of letting them know that the student is now in charge.

It’s a truly wonderful feeling. Even if this entire takeover is trash, I’m still proud to have been given this wonderful opportunity. That said, I did get an A in my GCSE English and English Lit!

To give some context: I am not a writer, nor an intellectual or a journalist. I am Femi Koleoso, a musician from north London. Born to Nigerian parents and raised in Enfield, a corner of London paved with gold, I started playing the drums at church (I know, typical). This became more than a hobby; it was a deep-set love, nurtured in the UK’s wonderful state school system and polished in powerful youth clubs. Today, I travel the world with my band, Ezra Collective, playing and producing music, DJing and broadcasting on BBC Radio 6 Music for a living. If there were a version of the “British-Nigerian dream” that didn’t involve becoming a lawyer, accountant or doctor, you could say my family and I got pretty close.

There’s power in a happy story; it brings hope. Normal school, amazing career. That’s the dream, right? That said, joy is at the centre of who I am, and every day I am filled with hope for the future.

But is there really reason to have hope for the future? Though I often only want to talk about Arsenal football club and playing the drums, I am well-informed enough to see the many reasons to lose all hope, not just for the future of the UK but the world. But while I acknowledge that, I believe there is a counter argument. I believe there is reason to have hope for the future of the UK and beyond; perhaps in this guest edit, I’m building a case for a more positive outlook on things.

The word “hope” has many definitions, but as my dear friend, the actor Letitia Wright, wonderfully phrases it via spoken-word interludes on our new album, Here Because of Hope, hope also captures the belief that on the other side of pain there can be renewal. There’s joy after mourning. Beauty from the ashes. Even when you don’t know how or when things will change, there can still be something inside you that believes your feet will eventually land on solid ground.

So on one side, you have pain; on the other, there will be joy. And hope is a marker on that spectrum that brings you from one end to the other; it makes you feel like getting to joy might be possible.

Being a musician, I see that hope most eloquently articulated in songs. Songs born out of pain bring joy. Fela Kuti wrote a song about his mother being executed by the Nigerian government – and its bassline became a club anthem. The pain and hardship of life in poverty-ridden council estates gave us grime music, which has people sweating and smiling in clubs. Calypso even emerged out of the horrors of the transatlantic slave trade.

The fuel for this wide-ranging artistic output, across continents and centuries is, for me, hope. In these features, you’ll be able to read about some people and stories that bring me out of pain and into joy; stories that bring me hope.

Collective decisions: Ezra’s cultural picks

Film: The Secret Agent

I watched The Secret Agent recently while on a long drive to a show in Italy. It’s an intense story and Wagner Moura is incredible. I love the way director Kleber Mendonça Filho so immersively takes you into 70s Brazil. TJ Koleoso

Album: Rosa Passos – Recriação

Recriação by Rosa Passos is a beautiful album, with minimal instrumentation but used in the most perfect way. Especially the drumming. It’s often just kick drum, rather than the full kit, and it works incredibly well. Also, if anybody knows what synth they used on the record, please let me know. Joe Armon-Jones

Live music: Southbank Centre

Rather than go the traditional album-film-TV-show route, I’m picking the Southbank Centre. As part of its 75th-anniversary celebrations, it chose to celebrate the steelpan, and I had the privilege of watching loads of young bands play. It was a “best of London” feeling just seeing so many different generations, cultures and people all dancing and celebrating the joy that togetherness and music can bring. Femi Koleoso

Film: My Father’s Shadow

My pick is Akinola Davies Jr’s 2025 film My Father’s Shadow, a Nigerian coming-of-age tale. I watched it recently and loved it. The storytelling was great and it felt so raw. It had so much cultural depth, which I could resonate with as a Nigerian. Ife Ogunjobi

EntertainmentTab.title: ‘The first half of my 20s was hell’: Maisie Williams on her tough childhood and why she’s been having more fun since Game of Thrones
EntertainmentTab.text:
Maisie Williams has dabbled in witchcraft exactly once. The actor was getting ready to audition for a part in a film. “I wanted it so badly that I went on to Etsy, and I paid a witch to manifest me the role,” she says, poker-faced.

“It didn’t work, and that was where my days of witchcraft ended,” she adds, breaking into an infectious cackle.

The spell may not have worked that time, but Williams will soon try her own hand at witchcraft on screen in Practical Magic 2. The sequel to the beloved 1998 romcom, about two supernatural sisters played by Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman, it features Williams as Antonia, the youngest daughter of Bullock’s Sally Owens. She never did get her money back from her Etsy witch. “It was maybe, like, £16.50? Which is not going to break the bank, but good for her. Good for her, to be making money doing nothing!” Williams laughs again.

We meet on a sweltering afternoon at a posh pub in Belgravia in London where women in expensive-looking sundresses are drinking Aperol spritzes on the terrace. Williams arrives from a busy day of appointments. She removes a pair of oversized grey headphones and sets them down on the table (she was listening to the US singer-songwriter Slayyyter on the walk over). “I’m in my business outfit because I’ve had business meetings,” she explains. (It’s arguably a very gen Z take on corporate dressing: long, dark hair worn in a practical ponytail, white T-shirt, smart grey trousers with a matching grey miniskirt attached, chunky, don’t‑mess-with-me Prada boots.)

Today’s agenda has included two jewellery fittings for a red carpet event, an “important producing meeting, with me as the producer” and lunch with her former Game of Thrones co-star Hannah Murray. The pair were catching up and discussing Murray’s recent memoir, The Make-Believe, about her devastating experience with a wellness cult. The group promised spiritual healing through expensive, elaborate rituals; Murray experienced a psychotic episode and was later diagnosed with bipolar disorder. “I knew something was going on, but I didn’t know it was that,” Williams says. “I felt really upset with myself for not asking sooner.”

Williams says she hasn’t always been a sceptic regarding magic. “I used to indulge in the whimsy of the patterns of the universe and think, ‘Oh, it’s a sign that everything’s going to work out.’” She says, taking a sip of Diet Coke. But after reading Murray’s book, Williams decided that searching for symbols in daily life might not be so wholesome after all. “I realised it leaves your mind slightly malleable to seeing a sign because you think it’s a divine intervention, and not just a good, fun coincidence.”

The 29-year-old actor is probably still best known as Arya Stark from Game of Thrones, the baby-faced assassin who shot her to stratospheric levels of fame at age 12. I remember first seeing her in Carol Morley’s The Falling, in which she stood out as a prickly, stiff‑backed schoolgirl opposite a then unknown Florence Pugh. In the seven years since Game of Thrones ended, Williams has landed roles in Marvel spin-off The New Mutants, in Danny Boyle’s miniseries Pistol as punk icon Jordan, and in Apple TV’s The New Look, a glossy drama about Christian Dior and Coco Chanel in Nazi-occupied Paris. She has started her own production company, and co-hosts the Frank Film Club podcast with two of her friends. It has been a period of trying different things, of searching for light relief, after a long stretch dealing with some much darker stuff. Last year, she even got a new agent. “He was bringing me fun things and was calling me every day,” she says. One of those fun, unexpected things was Practical Magic 2.

Williams had seen the original once or twice, but rewatched it before her audition. “The first movie has a lot of different beats to it,” she says diplomatically. That’s one way to put it: tonally, the film is all over the place. Based on an Alice Hoffman novel, it tells the story of the Owens sisters, two witches doomed by an ancestral curse: any man who falls in love with an Owens woman is destined to die. It is a cult classic, with fabulous 90s costumes, Bullock and Kidman drunkenly dancing around their kitchen to Harry Nilsson’s Coconut and a jarringly dark domestic violence subplot. The sequel is much slicker. Directed by Susanne Bier, it sends Sally’s more rebellious eldest daughter Kylie (Joey King) to England as she tries to break the family curse. Bullock and Kidman go after her, bickering the whole way, while Williams’s character, a trainee neurosurgeon, holds the fort at home.

“Sandra Bullock and Nicole Kidman are real movie stars – from a time in cinema that is escaping us,” says Williams matter-of-factly. “I went into this film seeing them as otherworldly.” She recalls meeting the actors for the first time at the read-through. Later that day she was heading to Glastonbury festival. “I got back in my car, and I wound the windows up, and I was just like … ” Williams claps both French-manicured hands to her face and lets out a high-pitched shriek. “I had my dog in the car. He was probably thinking, ‘What is going on?!’ And then I drove to Glastonbury.” On set, in between takes, the veteran Hollywood actors imparted important wisdom to their younger co-stars. But it wasn’t about the industry. “We spoke about how being friends with your ex is a fallacy,” she says. Who said that? Was it Kidman, who is recently divorced? “We all said that!” Williams demurs.

In the film, Williams and King are an inseparable sister duo, snuggled under the covers at their mum’s house and whispering as if they’re at a sleepover. In real life, Williams has three siblings, including one sister who is five years her senior. “When we’re together it’s like no time has passed but we’re not … ” She pauses. “We don’t call every day,” she says. “We’ve had waves in our life when we’re a lot closer, but a lot of our connection now comes through the kids.” Williams takes her niece and nephew on camping trips. “We never went out partying together,” she says. And, anyway, when she would have been the right age, Williams was busy filming Game of Thrones. “I was away most of the time, and I’d moved out as well.”

Williams’s route to child stardom came via a curiously X Factor-themed school nativity play. “I played Sharon Osbourne, and had done such a good job that my friend’s mum felt compelled to tell my mum, ‘You should put her into classes.’ That was when I started taking it seriously, because they were taking me seriously.” Then things got very serious, with Williams barely in secondary school when she landed a role on Game of Thrones. The speed at which her career took off shaped her expectations of the film industry, she says. “I thought, oh! Whatever you want, you can get. Like that,” she says, snapping her fingers. “That was how I thought the industry was.” Her naivety, she reckons, was a good thing. “It informed the way I see life, and the way I threw myself into what turned out to be a huge responsibility.”

Those early positive experiences, she says, gave her the confidence to pursue her dreams. “I wasn’t knocked down as a child. I wasn’t knocked down by my mum. I wasn’t knocked down by teachers at drama school, and I wasn’t knocked down by the industry when I did start auditioning.” Williams wonders if she would have still been resilient if she hadn’t enjoyed early success. “I think that a lot of people have a gift, but they just don’t get cast in a huge TV show when they’re 12.”

Williams claims not to know about an Arya Stark spin-off movie that is reportedly in development with HBO. “I saw that, too! I was like, huh?” Would she be interested in returning to that character? “I don’t know, really. She would have to be developed in some way because I feel like I’ve changed so much, and I feel like what people loved about Arya is that she was always a child doing things that were quite grownup.”

In person, Williams is warm but somewhat guarded; she sits next to me on the leather banquette but maintains a cautious distance. She is good company, with a beaming smile and a glorious, trilling laugh, but several times in our conversation I sense her weighing up her words. When asked about her early life growing up between Bristol and Somerset she becomes visibly uncomfortable. She settles on an honest, abridged answer. “My mum and my siblings and I spent a lot of time with my auntie,” she says, adding that she was mostly raised by the two women. “My auntie was a childminder with loads of other kids, so my life was vibrant and silly and fun and playful.”

Williams describes herself as “not coming from a hugely privileged background”. I wonder how, on the brink of 30, she reflects on growing up with less. “When I reflect on myself as a child, I wish I could just tell her it’s going to be fine. It’s going to work out. I think the fear that I felt at that time was so defining for many years of my childhood. I didn’t know. I was so ambitious as a small child, and I think maybe that did come from wanting my life to be different.”

In 2022, Williams spoke about the difficulties she faced back then on the Diary of a CEO podcast. Her parents split up when she was a baby, and her father is no longer in her life. “I had a traumatic relationship with my dad, and ever since I can remember I have struggled sleeping,” she told host Steven Bartlett. She described a teacher noticing her struggling at school and asking if she ate breakfast in the mornings. Williams said she didn’t. She was eight. The teacher called her mum. “I would look around at other kids and be, like, ‘Why don’t they seem to understand this pain or dread or fear? Joy – when does that come for me?” she said on the podcast.

“I have very close friends that I had not told,” Williams says today. “What I said on that podcast was all I’ve said about it to a lot of people, other than my family and my therapist. I even had boyfriends who didn’t know. So my reluctance to want to talk about it again is because my relationship to fame, and my relationship to success, was hugely defined by my childhood experience, and so that being explored in such a public setting now feels a little bit … terrifying?” She winces.

“I think it reached a lot of people who were in the same position, and I’m really happy that it did.” I’m curious to know why she chose that moment to finally speak about what had happened to her. “I always wanted to,” she says. “I think part of the reason why I was so good at playing Arya was because of how I’d grown up.”

She says journalists would often ask her how she was able to access such difficult emotions as a younger, less experienced actor. “I always felt like it was something I couldn’t say. I could access these emotions because I felt them myself, every one of them, for really extended periods of time.” What emotions? “Anger and fear.” She lets out a bitter laugh. “Stonewalling. I know that feeling of shutting down. These things that you don’t really start to understand about yourself until a lot later.” Being a teenager, she says, is already so fraught with emotion.

By the time she recorded that podcast, “I had done a lot of therapy,” she says, “and so was feeling a lot clearer about a lot of things.” It was Bartlett’s initial question that cracked them open for her. “He said, ‘What happened to you as a child that defines how you are?’ or something. It’s literally the only question that someone would have to ask me for me to answer honestly.” I was struck by her candour and vulnerability in that interview, I tell her. “I just thought that by releasing it, it was the last step in being free from it. Which kind of turned out to be true,” she says.

I wonder what she makes of Bartlett now. “Mmm,” she says, eyebrows raising, her mouth tightening into a horizontal line. In recent years, Bartlett has become a controversial figure, who has been criticised for amplifying medical misinformation and platforming manosphere-adjacent guests such as fellow podcaster Chris Williamson, who blamed declining birthrates on “women’s socioeconomic emancipation into the workforce”. Bartlett has aired the views of “experts” who claimed that Covid vaccines were “a net negative for society” and that cancer could be treated by a keto diet. It’s not a show that seems particularly aligned with liberal values.

“At the time, it felt like he had a podcast that felt fresh and different,” Williams says. “After, I felt slightly like I had been part of a podcast that gets a lot of views based on uprooting trauma. When I saw the trailer to the episode, I felt slightly icked out by how he had clipped it. But ultimately I can’t control that. Now I just feel like it’s quite dangerous, some of these conversations that are being had and taken out of context.”

Still, speaking about her experiences publicly was “a huge, defining moment of change” for Williams. “The first half of my 20s was just hell, but I think maybe it is for a lot of people,” she says. “I think that has more to do with the fact that Game of Thrones was ending, and I didn’t know what I was going to do next, and I just needed a break, to be honest with you. And then it also has to do with delayed teenage awkward years, and figuring a lot of things out that I felt like maybe I couldn’t do much earlier than that. And also Covid, and also an industry strike,” she adds with a shrug. The pub is getting noisy, filling up with finance bros who have just finished work.

“But post-2023, every day has been getting better,” she says. What happened in 2023? “I started seeing my friends again. I moved out of London. I was living alone. I was back with my dog. Everything was different,” she says. Williams is too discreet to confirm whether this change was sparked by the breakup of her long‑term relationship with fashion designer Reuben Selby. “At that point, it was time to … ” She smiles as if she’s got a secret. “Just choose myself,” she says. “What always comes into my mind is Kim Cattrall,” she adds, paraphrasing a quote the actor gave to the Guardian that became a popular meme. “‘I don’t want to be anywhere, not even for an hour, where I’m not enjoying myself.’ That’s truly how I’ve been the last three years.”

For Williams, choosing herself means “a lot of quiet, a lot of reading, and writing, and yoga, and running, and exercise, and swimming, and cycling, and walking the dog. Walking the dog for, like, hours a day.” In other words, being in her body. “Exactly, because then I know what I want. And that can be going out with my friends all weekend, or it can be a fun dinner in London where you miss your last train home, or it can be going to the cinema alone.” This summer, it has meant going to Primavera Sound and seeing singer Ethel Cain play, having barbecues with her friends and watching the World Cup in her local pub.

When I ask Williams what her career ambitions are now, a misty, faraway look comes over her. She does say her dreams out loud, but she’d rather not say them in print, she says. “My ambition is to work with people who have proven themselves to be really talented,” she says. “I’ve worked in the industry for quite a long time, and even though I love working with debut directors, there’s a stark difference in our experience now, which is noticeable. Working with people who are more experienced brings a different atmosphere on set.” She’s also been pouring her time into her production company, Rapt. It has meant reading a lot of scripts. “I cannot tell you the amount of postpartum horrors that people are making,” she says. “Whenever there’s one great movie, you’ll get seven scripts like that on your desk.” She and her co-founder, Lowri Roberts, are having fun writing their own feature film, too. “It’s a dark comedy. It’s a satire about the end of the world,” she says.

Williams has frequently been cast in dark, dramatic roles: “But I don’t really think that’s how I am most of the time,” she says. “I think when I’m in bad situations, I’d be more likely to laugh than to cry. I don’t know if I’m really in the camp of ‘plan for the worst’. I’ve had periods of my life where I’ve been so overcome by the fear of what could go wrong that, particularly now, I’m more in a phase of ‘anything can be fixed’.”

Not that there’s much that needs fixing. She is dating and “so happy” about it, though she is coy when pressed about the details. Has she been enjoying playing the field? “No! I’m in love,” she says, smirking. “That’s all I’ll say.” Does it feel different from other times she’s been in love? “Yes, which is good. There’s lots of laughter,” she says, giggling. The vibe this summer, she says, has been “hot, in all senses of the word”. She grins. “I got myself a fan. I am a late adopter of the fan.” Before that, she says, she was “just sweating”. These days, she’s too busy enjoying herself a la Kim Cattrall to be constantly bracing for the worst. “Life is actually quite fun, but we all torture ourselves over the agony of what could be.”

GeneralTab.title: Russia-Ukraine war: US envoys begin Ukraine talks after Putin meeting
GeneralTab.text:
President Volodymyr Zelensky is holding talks with Donald Trump's top envoys, in their first visit to Ukraine since Russia's full-scale invasion.

The Ukrainian leader greeted Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at Kyiv's St Sophia Cathedral, close to where a Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine's security services on Friday.

Ahead of the meeting, Zelensky said Ukraine was ready to talk about bringing "the end of the war closer". But he said security guarantees would be required as well as a dignified post-war peace.

On Saturday, the two envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow for talks on ending the war that were described as "frank" and "constructive" by the Kremlin.

The envoys travelled to Kyiv by train after flying to Poland – Zelensky told the media that it was not possible for them to land their plane despite preparations.

Putin and Zelensky agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days while the negotiators carry out their trip.

While Witkoff and Kushner were in talks at the Kremlin on Saturday, Zelensky said he and his team were "ready for a substantive conversation".

On Sunday, Zelensky wrote on social media that his country "has always been and will remain constructive".

"We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed.

"A dignified character of the postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are ready," he said.

Overnight, Russian and Ukrainian forces continued to exchange strikes, with Ukraine confirming they struck an oil refinery, an airfield, and two air defence systems.

The country's defence ministry said they targeted the Ryazan oil refinery, which supplies the Russian army, and an airfield in Rostov-on-Don.

Earlier, Ukraine's Air Force reported that Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 long-range drones and small cruise missiles.

The country's air defences downed 82 drones and six missiles, but 11 locations were hit, with debris falling at a further seven sites.

GeneralTab.title: Business secretary to meet Jaguar Land Rover boss as thousands of job cuts expected
GeneralTab.text:
Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds will meet the bosses of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) and the Unite union to discuss the impact of thousands of expected job cuts at the car maker.

JLR confirmed to the BBC it is opening a voluntary redundancy programme, a year on from a cyber attack which brought production to a halt for more than a month.

The company did not confirm the numbers but the Times reported as many as 4,000 jobs may be lost due to the impact of tariffs and a drop in sales.

Reynolds told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg the meeting early next week will focus on ways to "mitigate any job losses" but ruled out a bailout for the company.

Asked about the cuts, which are believed to impact mainly white collar workers, Reynolds said: "A company the size of JLR, which is a huge British success story, at various times in its business cycle, the number of, directly, people it employs will change.

"If this is about making sure over time that the workforce is right to make the business as competitive as possible, that's the conversation we need to have."

He said there would be no support "if it's to bail people out", but opened the door to a "long-term investment in the future" of the company.

The cuts come as Chancellor John Healey is preparing to deliver a speech in the Midlands on Monday promising to boost economic growth by changing how the government values investment in infrastructure such as transport and housing. JLR is based in Coventry, in the West Midlands.

JLR has not confirmed the scale of the job cuts, but said they would "simplify" the business and "improve efficiency and build greater resilience".

"Today, we informed our colleagues, and trade union partners that JLR is opening a voluntary redundancy programme offering salaried and management team members the opportunity to leave the business," a spokesperson said.

"We will share further information with our colleagues first." It did not rule out the prospect of some compulsory redundancies as part of the plans.

Unite general secretary Sharon Graham said the union had been warning about a "perfect storm" hanging over the automotive industry for some time.

"Death by a thousand cuts has been going on under the nose of successive governments," she said.

She added there had been "intensive" discussions over the weekend about mitigating jobs losses.

Reynolds was asked about the impact on the car industry of the UK's electric vehicle sales target, which means manufacturers must ensure a percentage of the cars they sell each year are zero emissions, with the target rising each year to reach 80% by 2030.

He said one of the first things he had done as business secretary was give the industry more flexibility to work towards that and said there was a further consultation open on it.

"It's not where it needs to be and that's why we're willing to change the regulation to work with where consumer demand is and the industry," he added.

He said he had also spoken with West Midlands mayor Richard Parker about supporting the business and its staff.

JLR in July said fewer than 300 people would leave the firm under cost savings plans announced at the time.

It employs about 30,000 people in its UK operations, with approximately 10,000 people employed at plants overseas.

The cyber attack in September 2025 led to the shut down of all manufacturing at JLR for several weeks, meaning not a single vehicle rolled off its production lines.

That led to a 27% drop in overall production at the company, which is one of the West Midlands' biggest employers.

The overall cost of the cyber-attack and the subsequent loss of manufacturing was estimated to be £1.9bn.

In June, the firm announced it planned to cut about £1.7bn in costs over the coming years to help towards its recovery from the attack.

JLR had indicated at the time that it would make the savings through cuts in areas such as materials, warranty and fixed costs.

Additional reporting by Simon Jack

GeneralTab.title: Anak Krakatau: Volcano eruption closes six Indonesian airports
GeneralTab.text:
More than 150,000 passengers have been left stranded after a volcanic eruption forced Indonesian authorities to temporarily suspend operations at eight airports.

Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport was the first to be closed on Sunday morning after ash from Anak Krakatau was detected in airspace near the airport.

Transport minister Dudy Purwagandhi said so far 712 flights have been affected and asked airlines to consider diverting some flights to other airports.

The volcano had started erupting late on Friday night, generating continuous seismic activity, lava fountains, and booming sounds across surrounding regions. Two more eruptions happened early on Sunday, authorities said.

The transport ministry said the pause in operations mainly affected flights to and from Singapore, also other international routes including Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur.

Purwagandhi said the decision to temporarily close more airports was made after tests found that volcanic ash had spread towards West Java.

He urged airlines to speed up processes for refunding tickets for passengers who have been affected by flight cancellations, and for airlines to provide timely information to those with upcoming flights to avoid overcrowding at airports.

According to Indonesia's meteorological agency BMKG, ash reached as far as 20,000ft (6,000m) on Java on east of the volcano, and 50,000ft (15,000m) west of the volcano on the Sumatra side.

Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano, which is in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra.

The health minister has urged residents in affected areas to stay indoors and wear face masks to protect against respiratory, eye, and skin risks.

According to local newspaper Kompas, several schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents reported eye irritations from the ash, while some fishermen had cancelled fishing trips at sea similarly reporting sore eyes.

One resident, Aldi Candra Prayogi, told the outlet that he felt since Friday evening and it felt like "small grains of sand had gotten into my eyes", and that he needs to use eye drops to ease the irritation.

The dust is so thick that he has to sweep the front yard of his house every five minutes, he also said.

Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa.

The volcano - also known as Anak Krakatoa - collapsed in December 2018, triggering a huge tsunami which killed over 400 people, and displaced and injured thousands more on the nearby coastlines of Sumatra and Java.

Scientists found that some of the chunks of rock that slid from the volcano when it collapsed were about 70-90m high.

The Pacific Ring of Fire refers to a string of volcanoes, earthquake sites and tectonic plates around the Pacific. It spreads across 40,000km (25,000 miles) from the southern tip of South America all the way to New Zealand.

Roughly 90% of all earthquakes occur along the area and the ring is dotted with 75% of all active volcanoes on Earth, that's 452 individual active volcanoes.

GeneralTab.title: Trump calls for interest rate cut after jobs figures raise hike bets
GeneralTab.text:
Donald Trump has called for interest rates to be cut later this month, claiming higher rates put the US at a "very unfair disadvantage".

The president's remarks came as stronger-than-expected jobs figures in the US added to growing expectations that rates could be increased, with inflation still running high and American households feeling the pinch of rising prices.

The number of roles added to the economy increased by 162,000 in August, almost triple the 56,000 forecast by analysts, driven by a boost in hospitality and education hiring.

Trump said the US should have the "LOWEST RATE of any country in the World".

"The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart - BE PATRIOTS for a change. High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won't allow that to happen!", the president said in a post on social media, external.

Last week, Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US central bank, signalled that rates could be hiked if policymakers were not confident price rises were easing for Americans.

Inflation, which measures price increases over time, remains above the Fed's 2% annual target, with prices up 3.4% in the past 12 months, according to the latest data.

The next interest rate decision will be made on 15-16 September. Rates were left unchanged between 3.5% and 3.75% in July for the fifth time in a row, but concerns over inflation remain due to the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, which has caused as surge in global oil prices.

On Friday, US diesel prices hit an all-time high of $5.85 a gallon on average, compared to $3.71 a year ago.

But despite the cost of living rising, wages also appear to be increasing. In August, average hourly earnings for all employees were $37.75 on average, having increased 3.1%.

"Even the most committed dove would struggle to find anything in the August employment report to justify keeping interest rates unchanged," said Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics.

He added that the strength in the jobs market meant that the latest inflation figures released next week would only need to be moderately above the Fed's target to fuel expectations of a September hike.

"A hike in rates just became a bit more likely," said Neil Birrell, chief investment office of investment firm Premier Miton.

Almost 60% of traders were betting on an interest rate hike in September, according to CME Group's "FedWatch" data.

An increase in employment during the final month of the summer in restaurants and bars, as well as in local government education ahead of the new school year, was behind August's labour market rebound.

Weaker job figures released earlier in the summer were revised up by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, revealing a stronger labour market than previously thought. Instead of the economy being deemed to have shed 23,000 jobs in July, some 44,000 were found to have been created in subsequent estimates.

While many more jobs were added, the US unemployment rate remained unchanged at 4.1% last month, with seven million out of work. Both measures have changed little over the year.

In response to the stronger jobs figures raising expectations of a interest rate hike, US stock market indexes were trading down on Friday.

Trump called the response "crazy". "We just got GREAT Numbers on Jobs, the Market should go UP, because our Credit and Economy are better but, as always, for the past 25 years, the Stock Market goes DOWN, because we're living under False Reality that if things are good, you've got to "KILL IT" because of a "fear" of Inflation," he said.

GeneralTab.title: Jackdaw gas field set to be approved as soon as mid-September, sources say
GeneralTab.text:
The UK government is set to give the go-ahead for a controversial new gas field off the coast of Aberdeen, the BBC understands.

Approval for the Jackdaw project could come in mid-September, just before Parliament breaks for party conference season, according to government and industry sources.

The gas field was approved by the former Conservative government in 2022 but was delayed by a legal ruling from a Scottish court, after environmental groups argued consent was given without fully considering the climate impact.

Jackdaw's owner says it will account for 6% of UK gas output when at peak production but environmental groups say it will provide only 2% of UK use when imports are included.

Campaigners launched legal challenges after Jackdaw was approved in 2022 and when the Rosebank oil field off Shetland was given the green light in 2023.

The Court of Session in Edinburgh ruled last year that Rosebank and Jackdaw had been unlawfully approved because the government had failed to take into account the climate impact of burning extracted oil and gas from the sites.

A judge ruled that more detailed climate assessments had to be published, and further estimates were put out for consultation in July.

Both Jackdaw and Rosebank are operated by Adura, a joint venture between energy giants Shell and Norway's Equinor. Aberdeen-based firm Ithaca also owns 20% of Rosebank.

Adura has estimated that Jackdaw could produce 35.8m tonnes of carbon over its 11-year lifetime, the equivalent of 90% of Scotland's emissions for 2023. But it said a more likely estimate was about 23.6m tonnes - equivalent to 60% of the 2023 figure.

Environmentalists insist that more drilling would be unconscionable, hampering efforts to cut planet-warming carbon emissions as deadly heatwaves and extreme weather affect billions across the globe.

They also say starting production would not protect energy security and that transitioning sooner to greener technologies would be better for supporting jobs.

But industry bodies argue that starting production at the sites would provide much-needed jobs and improve the UK's energy security as overseas conflicts threaten supply.

Advocates of the project also told the BBC that Jackdaw's output is critical to extending the life of other North Sea infrastructure including Shearwater - a large offshore oil and gas production hub that processes hydrocarbons before piping them to coastal refineries and terminals.

Adura said that if approval comes in September, the field could start delivering gas to UK homes by this winter as the construction is "99% complete".

A public consultation on the future of Jackdaw and another new oil field, Rosebank, closed in August and the decision now rests with Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh.

Speaking in the House of Commons on Thursday, Energy Minister Kate White said that the energy secretary would make separate decisions on the two sites, but gave no indication of the timings of an announcement.

"The process ended in August, and the Secretary of State will be taking those decisions in due course," she told MPs.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently said there needs to be a "pragmatic approach" towards domestic oil and gas.

"We won't be able to stop using oil and gas for some time. That's just a fact," he said.

"The question is whether we can accelerate use of it so that we pay for the transition."

Tessa Khan, executive director of environmental group Uplift which brought the legal challenge, said more North Sea drilling would not cut energy bills and would "make no meaningful difference" to UK energy supply.

"The science is clear that the world already has far more oil and gas than can ever be safely burned if we are to limit warming," she added.

"When it comes to these decisions, the prime minister needs to listen to scientists warnings and think back to those families who lost their homes to this summer's wildfires, the UK farmers struggling to grow our food in the drought, and the lives lost in the floods in Nepal – and not the self-interested demands of the oil companies."

The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero said it does not comment on speculation.

A spokesman added: "The North Sea remains a vital national asset and oil and gas will continue to play an important role in our energy system for decades to come - alongside transitioning to clean power to protect jobs and tackle the climate crisis.

"Any decision will take into account all relevant evidence, including environmental assessments and public representations received during the consultation process."

"We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. Peace is needed. Security guarantees are needed.

"A dignified character of the postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are ready," he said.

Overnight, Russian and Ukrainian forces continued to exchange strikes, with Ukraine confirming they struck an oil refinery, an airfield, and two air defence systems.

The country's defence ministry said they targeted the Ryazan oil refinery, which supplies the Russian army, and an airfield in Rostov-on-Don.

Earlier, Ukraine's Air Force reported that Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 long-range drones and small cruise missiles.

The country's air defences downed 82 drones and six missiles, but 11 locations were hit, with debris falling at a further seven sites.
